# eMethods 2. What was verified, and what verification cannot establish

Analyses of administrative data are usually described in terms of the sources
consumed and the exclusions applied. That description is necessary and it is
not sufficient: it says what the analyst intended, not what the code did. This
appendix documents the second question. It states the properties the pipeline
is required to hold, how each is checked, one defect the checks found before it
reached any reported figure, and — at the end, in more detail than is
conventional — what these checks do **not** establish.

None of the machinery described here changed a single reported estimate. That
is a result rather than an omission, and where a number could have moved and did
not, it is said so explicitly.

## Properties the pipeline is required to hold

Ten properties are declared in a machine-readable registry
(`tests/science_law_registry.tsv`) and evaluated nightly. They are stated as
properties of the *answer* rather than as unit tests of functions, because a
function can be individually correct while the composition of several is wrong.

| | Property |
|---|---|
| L1 | Every artifact declaring a cohort size declares a registered one. A superseded cohort vintage cannot silently return. |
| L2 | Population is conserved. Parts sum to their whole, and no share exceeds its declared denominator. |
| L3 | Missing geography stays missing. A record with no usable ZIP is never assigned a county. |
| L4 | More travel time cannot reduce measured access. |
| L5 | Every routed provider appears in the dissolved access surface. |
| L6 | Masking evidence cannot invent geography. Degrading an input can only degrade the answer. |
| L7 | Contradictory identity evidence cannot increase certainty. |
| L8 | Identical inputs produce identical outputs. |
| L9 | A cache may change runtime, not the answer. |
| L10 | Every mutable scientific input has a declared vintage. |

Each property must satisfy five conditions, and the build fails if any is
absent: it is registered; it is actually evaluated; it is evaluated on a
non-zero number of subjects; it carries a *positive control* demonstrating that
its detector responds to a violation; and it carries a deliberately planted
defect that it detects. Thirty defects are planted across the ten
properties and all thirty are detected.

The fourth condition is the one that is usually missing. A check that reports
"no violations found" has demonstrated that it did not fire. It has not
demonstrated that it *could* fire, and those two states are indistinguishable in
a passing build. An inert check is worse than no check, because it is credited
as reassurance.

## Two properties, stated as scientific claims

**L6 — masking evidence cannot invent geography.** This property exists because
its violation occurred. An earlier version of the ZIP-to-county crosswalk
grouped Census records by ZIP without first excluding the 903 rows that carry no
ZIP code. Those rows collapsed to a single key of missing value, and because a
left join matches a missing key to a missing key, every subject with no usable
ZIP was assigned that row's county — a real, remote, rural county in Alaska.
Absent geography was not merely mishandled; it was converted into a specific
and plausible location, and it carried a rurality classification into downstream
estimates. The property is now checked by masking 400 real Census ZIP codes in
sixteen ways and asserting that no masked subject acquires a county. Its planted
defect is the historical bug itself, rebuilt.

**L7 — contradictory identity evidence cannot increase certainty.** Linkage in
this study rests on name comparison (Appendix 1). The governing requirement is
therefore directional: removing or contradicting evidence must never produce a
*more* confident match. This is checked against a frozen corpus of adversarial
identity cases.

The same principle decided the design of the fix described next, and it is worth
stating plainly because it is not intuitive: **narrowing a study frame must
never widen its answer.**

## A defect found before it reached any reported figure

The deterministic license-resolution routine reported that it had resolved
`3 of 2` certificants — 150.0% — for a two-person roster.

The percentage was the symptom. The defect was that the set of deterministic
matches was constructed from every qualifying identifier in the state-license
file, and the roster the routine had been asked about was consulted only
afterwards. A person outside the declared study population was therefore
resolved, counted, and written to the output artifact as a finding about that
population. Four of the routine's six audit metrics were affected, reporting
400%, 150% and 250% of their denominator.

**No reported estimate is affected.** No artifact from this routine has ever
been committed to the repository, and the routine has no caller in the
production pipeline; it is reached only by its test suite. There was nothing to
regenerate. The defect was latent and would have corrupted the first production
run.

The repair is worth documenting because the obvious version of it is wrong. The
natural fix — restrict the license file to the roster before resolving — would
have introduced a more serious error than the one it removed. Two certificants
in the test fixture share a single board license key, so that key identifies
nobody and neither resolves. Filtering the license file to a roster containing
only the first would delete the second's record, the key would then appear
unique, and the first would resolve. The routine would have gained certainty
that existed only because the contradicting evidence had been removed — the
failure that L6 and L7 exist to forbid.

The restriction is therefore applied to the *claim* and never to the *evidence*.
Collision and cardinality checks continue to run against the entire external
license universe, because that universe is the evidence about whether a key
identifies one person. Only the set of people the routine may report on is
restricted, and restricting a claim can remove people but never add them.
Resolutions falling outside the frame are retained as an explicitly labelled
diagnostic rather than discarded, since they remain valid evidence about the
external universe and are merely not findings about this study population.

## Reproducibility of the computation itself

Three properties address whether the computation is stable and whether its
inputs are known.

**Determinism (L8).** Rebuilding from identical inputs must produce identical
outputs. Order of input records must not affect any result.

**Cache isolation (L9).** A cache may change how long a computation takes; it
may not change what the computation returns.

**Declared vintage (L10).** L8 and L9 establish that the computation is
deterministic *given* its inputs. L10 establishes that the inputs are known.
This was not previously true. Geocoding coordinates determine counties, and
counties determine the rurality classification reported in the main analysis;
those coordinates come from a cache that is written to over time. Across 112
provenance records there were 105 distinct declared inputs and none was a cache.
Fourteen artifacts depend on the cache transitively and none declared it. The
pipeline computed its result as a function of its declared inputs *and whatever
the cache happened to hold*, while recording only the former — so two analysts
running identical code against identical declared inputs could legitimately
obtain different geography with nothing recording why.

The cache now carries a content-derived identity: a hash over the nine
scientifically relevant fields, insensitive to row and column order, with
access-time fields excluded by name because an identity that changed when the
cache was merely *read* would be useless.

This is not an argument for freezing the cache. A cache that resolves more
addresses next month is better evidence, and forbidding improvement would be a
worse policy than tolerating drift. A later snapshot is a **new declared
input** — visible, attributable, and a legitimate reason for a number to move.
The fourteen pre-existing artifacts are recorded as historical debt rather than
retrospectively stamped: they were built against a snapshot nobody recorded, and
assigning them a vintage now would assert a provenance that is not the one that
produced them.

## What these checks do not establish

This section is longer than is customary because the risk that a verification
appendix is read as a guarantee is real, and the specific limits matter more
than the general disclaimer.

**They do not validate the linkage against truth.** Every property here is
internal: it constrains the pipeline to be self-consistent, deterministic, and
honest about its inputs. None of them establishes that a linked
certificant–registry pair is the same human being. That question is addressed in
Appendix 1 and remains the binding constraint on every geographic statement in
this analysis. A pipeline can satisfy all ten properties while resting on a
systematically biased linkage.

**Linkage completeness differs sharply by certification status**, and this is
the limitation most likely to affect inference. Records for certificants whose
status is active link at a substantially higher rate than records for those
recorded as deceased. Any analysis stratified on or adjusted for status
inherits that differential, and no property described here detects it, because
a differentially incomplete linkage is perfectly self-consistent.

**They do not establish that the reported estimate is the right estimate.** L2
requires that parts sum to their whole; it does not ask whether the whole is the
correct denominator for the scientific question. L4 requires that access cannot
fall as travel time rises; it does not establish that the travel times are
correct.

**Absence of a violation is not evidence of correctness in an unchecked area.**
The registry states what is enforced. Properties not in it are not enforced, and
the registry's value is precisely that this cannot be inferred from a filename
or a comment.

**One property is not currently evaluated in the reference environment.** L5
requires a derived isochrone surface that is excluded from version control, so
on a clean checkout it does not run and the coverage check fails rather than
passing silently. This is the intended behaviour — a property that cannot be
evaluated is reported as unevaluated rather than credited as satisfied — but it
means L5's guarantee currently rests on local execution. It is recorded as open
debt.

That last point generalizes. Every figure in this appendix was verified in an
environment that happened to contain data a clean checkout does not, and the
discrepancy was found only when the checks were deliberately re-run in isolation.
Verification machinery is subject to the same failure it is built to detect: it
can report success because it was asked the question in a setting where the
answer was guaranteed.
